title: Give me two ideas for this gap

messages.text: Give me two ideas for this gap

context.label: Label smoothing hurts perplexity
context.digest: Label smoothing of value 0.1 hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

plan.goal: Generate two candidate ideas for the label-smoothing / perplexity gap.

args.instruction: The gap: label smoothing (e.g., 0.1) hurts perplexity — the model becomes more uncertain and reports worse perplexity — while improving downstream accuracy and BLEU. Generate two candidate ideas that engage with this tension: how to reconcile or exploit the fact that a model that scores worse on perplexity can still be a better model. One idea may improve label smoothing itself (e.g., a variant that keeps perplexity intact), the other may attack the premise (e.g., whether perplexity is even the right evaluation under label smoothing). Ground the ideas in what is actually published where possible.

steps.why: The user asked for two new candidates for the selected gap; generation with two distinct stances fits the request.

messages.text: I drafted two ideas that take opposite tacks on the same tension — that label smoothing at 0.1 makes the model report worse perplexity while still getting better accuracy and BLEU. The first keeps the smoothing but makes it a schedule, annealing ε back to zero late in training so the perplexity floor disappears while the downstream gains are kept. The second leaves training alone and attacks the evaluation instead: it subtracts the known uniform floor that smoothing injects before computing perplexity, so the "hurt" either dissolves as an artifact or isolates genuine degradation. They're shown beside this message; the gap itself is still marked open in the literature, so both are grounded in what's actually published.

context.label: De-Smoothed Perplexity: Score the Sharp Component, Not the Injected Floor
context.digest: Label smoothing's perplexity penalty is largely an arithmetic artifact of scoring a deliberately smoothed distribution against a one-hot target; subtract the known uniform floor before computing perplexity and the paradox either dissolves or isolates true degradation.

plan.goal: Deepen the selected idea, De-Smoothed Perplexity, into a stronger research proposal.

args.instruction: Deepen the selected idea 'De-Smoothed Perplexity: Score the Sharp Component, Not the Injected Floor'. Work through its load-bearing assumption (that train and eval targets are identical / that raw probabilities are comparable across training schemes) and its open questions, and turn the proposal into something more defensible and concrete: (1) resolve or bound the clipping bias when p(y) falls below the uniform floor alpha/K — is the relu-renormalize transform biased for genuinely uncertain predictions, and can a floor-adjusted likelihood or an alternative transform avoid that; (2) decide whether evaluation should use the training alpha or fit alpha on held-out data, and how to make that choice principled; (3) check whether the de-smoothed distribution is a proper scoring rule and what happens to decoding/beam-search rankings if it is used; (4) address what a residual gap after de-smoothing means — real degradation vs a temperature/calibration shift caused by smoothing, and how to disentangle them; (5) make the evaluation protocol concrete against named baselines, including the inverse-mixture correction q=(p-alpha*u)/(1-alpha) used in the sibling annealed-smoothing idea, and state what evidence would confirm or falsify the claim that de-smoothed PPL tracks BLEU/accuracy better than raw PPL. Keep the idea's core move — leaving training untouched and fixing the evaluation premise — but tighten its weakest parts.

steps.why: The user wants the selected idea pushed further; that is refinement of one idea already in context.

done_criteria: at least one refined version of the idea returned
the refined version addresses the open questions: clipping bias, fitted vs training alpha, proper scoring / decoding, and residual-gap interpretation
